title: How to Calculate Your Debt-to-Income Ratio
summary: A step-by-step walkthrough of the DTI formula, with a worked example and what to include.
seoTitle: How to Calculate Your Debt-to-Income Ratio | Clarity
metaDescription: Step-by-step guide to calculating your debt-to-income ratio, with a worked example and what counts as debt.
content:
Calculating your debt-to-income ratio (DTI) takes two numbers you likely already know: your gross monthly income and your monthly debt payments. Here is exactly how to do it.

What you need before you start

Gather your gross monthly income (before taxes) and a list of your recurring monthly debt payments — not your full budget, just the debt obligations.

The formula

DTI = total monthly debt payments ÷ gross monthly income × 100

A worked example

Example

Gross income: $6,000/month. Debts: $1,800 mortgage, $400 car payment, $150 credit card minimum = $2,350 total. DTI = $2,350 ÷ $6,000 × 100 = 39.2%.

What typically counts as a monthly debt

Housing payment (rent or mortgage), auto loans, student loans, minimum credit card payments, and other installment or personal loans generally count. Everyday expenses like groceries, utilities, and subscriptions typically do not.

How Clarity calculates this automatically

Once your income and debts are entered in Cash Flow, Clarity calculates your DTI for you — no manual math required. You can also try the free DTI calculator without creating an account.

title: What Debts Count Toward Your DTI Ratio?
summary: Not all monthly bills count toward DTI. Here is what lenders typically include — and what they usually leave out.
seoTitle: What Debts Count Toward Your DTI Ratio? | Clarity
metaDescription: Not all monthly bills count toward DTI. Here's what lenders typically include — and what they usually leave out.
content:
Your debt-to-income ratio only counts certain monthly obligations. Knowing which ones helps you estimate your DTI accurately before a lender does it for you.

Debts that typically count

Housing payment (rent or mortgage, including property taxes and insurance if escrowed), auto loans, student loans, minimum credit card payments, and personal or installment loans generally count toward DTI.

Debts that typically don't count

Utilities, groceries, insurance premiums paid separately, subscriptions, and everyday living expenses are generally excluded — DTI measures debt obligations, not total spending.

Example

Mortgage ✓, car loan ✓, student loan ✓, credit card minimum ✓ — all typically count. Electric bill ✗, groceries ✗, gym membership ✗, streaming subscriptions ✗ — these generally do not.

Gray areas

Items like co-signed debt, alimony, or child support obligations may or may not count depending on the lender and loan program. If you have obligations like these, it is worth confirming directly with your lender how they will be treated.

Why this matters

Knowing what counts helps you build an accurate picture of your DTI before applying. Try the free DTI calculator, or see how to calculate DTI step by step.

title: Front-End vs. Back-End DTI: What's the Difference?
summary: Front-end and back-end DTI measure different things. Here's how lenders use each one and why the difference matters.
seoTitle: Front-End vs. Back-End DTI: What's the Difference? | Clarity
metaDescription: Front-end and back-end DTI measure different things. Here's how lenders use each one and why the difference matters.
content:
When lenders talk about DTI, they sometimes mean one of two different measurements: front-end or back-end. Here is what separates them.

Front-end DTI (housing only)

Front-end DTI compares only your housing payment (rent or mortgage, often including taxes and insurance) to your gross monthly income.

Back-end DTI (all debts)

Back-end DTI is broader — it compares all of your monthly debt payments, including housing, to your gross monthly income. This is generally what people mean by "DTI" without qualification.

Why lenders look at both

Reviewing both figures may give a lender a fuller picture: front-end DTI focuses on housing affordability specifically, while back-end DTI captures your overall debt burden.

Example

Gross income: $6,000/month. Mortgage: $1,800 — front-end DTI = 30%. Add a $400 car payment and $150 credit card minimum — back-end DTI = ($1,800 + $400 + $150) ÷ $6,000 = 39.2%.

Typical ranges

Guidelines vary widely by lender and loan program, so there is no single universal cutoff — general industry ranges are often discussed, but always confirm current requirements with your specific lender. See what lenders typically review for more context.

Try it yourself

Use the free DTI calculator to see your own back-end DTI, or read how to calculate DTI step by step.

title: How to Improve Your DTI Before Applying for a Loan
summary: Practical ways to lower your debt-to-income ratio before you apply for a mortgage or other loan.
seoTitle: How to Improve Your DTI Before Applying for a Loan | Clarity
metaDescription: Practical ways to lower your debt-to-income ratio before you apply for a mortgage or other loan.
content:
A lower DTI generally gives you more flexibility when applying for a loan. Here are practical, general ways people work on theirs before applying — none of which guarantee a specific outcome.

Pay down high-balance debts first

Paying down balances that carry a monthly minimum payment — credit cards in particular — can reduce your total monthly debt obligation directly.

Avoid taking on new debt before applying

A new car loan or financed purchase adds a monthly payment right when you may be trying to lower your DTI — timing matters.

Increase documented income

Additional documented income (a raise, a second job, rental income) can lower DTI from the other side of the formula, though lenders may have specific requirements for how income is verified.

Consider timing your application

If a large debt is close to being paid off, waiting until it is gone before applying may meaningfully change your ratio.

Example

Gross income: $6,000/month. Current debts total $2,350 (39.2% DTI). Paying off a $200/month personal loan brings debts to $2,150 — new DTI = $2,150 ÷ $6,000 = 35.8%.

Track your progress

Use the free DTI calculator to check your ratio as your debts change, or track it automatically over time in Clarity's Dashboard. See also what debts count toward DTI.

These steps may help improve your DTI, but they do not guarantee loan approval or a specific outcome — always confirm current requirements with your lender.
